cues.text: 1973, UC Berkeley: a program called SPICE learns to simulate circuits.
Tonight that 1973 program wakes up, inside your browser.
Circuit Séance: a hand-drawn circuit is read into a SPICE netlist…
…and ngspice, Berkeley SPICE’s open-source heir compiled to WebAssembly, simulates it on your device.
No server, no install, no account. The demo makes zero network requests.
Hover the green-phosphor scope to read any instant…
…and the Spirit explains the trace with numbers measured from the simulation: τ = 1 ms = R × C.
New: possess a component. Pick C1 and its spirit takes the slider.
Drag it: ngspice re-runs on every move, and the dashed ghost is the circuit before possession.
C × 2.2 → τ × 2.2. The readout shows it live: 1 ms becomes 2.2 ms.
Now ÷10: the capacitor fills ten times faster.
Homework check: solve it by hand, then let the simulation grade you (±5 %).
A classic slip, τ = RC/2, gets caught: off by −50 %.
Fix it, check again: correct. A lab partner for every EE problem set.
Haunted Classics: famous circuits resurrected from old pages.
The 1972 NE555 timer: its capacitor saws between ⅓ and ⅔ of the supply.
Bill Hewlett’s 1939 Wien-bridge oscillator: a sine wave grows out of a 10 mV whisper.
Every label and every explanation also works in Chinese, fully offline, with no blocked services.
Bring your own key (Qwen-VL by default) to read photos of your own drawings.
The key stays in this browser and goes only to the provider you pick. The demo needs none.
We built it spec-first with Kiro: steering, an EARS requirements spec, a design and a linked task list.
Every requirement is a WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL line that tasks link back to.
Kiro implemented the tasks in headless waves and ticked them off.
Agent hooks fired on every save: lint, netlist tests, and a spirit-tone review that hunts for leaked keys.
When the free credits ran out, we finished by hand, and logged every hand-written file.
Circuit Séance · 电路招魂. Berkeley SPICE, resurrected in your browser.
